claims.text: Superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys is governed primarily by chemical-disorder-induced electron scattering.
Chemical disorder suppresses the superconducting transition temperature relative to structurally similar low-entropy alloys.
Increased atomic-site disorder enhances electron scattering.
Enhanced electron scattering reduces the electron mean free path.
A reduced electron mean free path weakens Cooper pairing.
Increasing the number of principal elements while holding structure and electron count similar systematically increases compositional entropy.
Compositional entropy or site-occupancy randomness can quantify the degree of atomic-site disorder.
Chemical disorder reduces the electron-phonon coupling necessary for superconductivity.
Higher-compositional-entropy alloys will have lower superconducting transition temperatures than matched low-entropy analogs.
Higher-compositional-entropy alloys will have lower superconducting volume fractions than matched low-entropy analogs.
Matching crystal structure and electron count and minimizing extrinsic defects isolates the proposed chemical-disorder effect.
The proposed governing mechanism may not apply when strong electron correlations or magnetic impurities dominate.
Annealing the samples eliminates extrinsic defects.
Disorder-induced electron scattering in alloys is a general principle that makes the hypothesis plausible.
Electron mean free path can be inferred from resistivity measurements.
A failure of transition temperature and superconducting volume fraction to decrease with compositional entropy, or equal or higher values in the HEAs, would falsify the hypothesis.
